why_how.text: Every official sign, signal and marking must be obeyed unless an officer or road worker directs you differently.
Because each sign family has its own color and shape, you can name a sign before you can read it, such as the red square for Do Not Enter.

scenario.text: Maya reaches a red eight-sided sign at a quiet corner, and a walker is in the unmarked crosswalk.

reasoning.text: An octagon means stop, and a stop sign requires a complete stop, yielding, and waiting for anyone in a marked or unmarked crosswalk.

result.text: Maya stops completely, waits for the walker to finish crossing, and enters only when it is safe.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a yield sign always demands a full stop, just like a stop sign.

correction.text: A yield sign asks you to slow down and give the right of way, and you stop only when traffic or pedestrians make it necessary.

memory_support.text: Eight sides stop, three sides yield, the red square keeps you out.

prompt.text: You turn onto a ramp and face a square red sign reading Do Not Enter. What is the likely problem?

answer.text: You are probably heading the wrong way, and you must not enter.

rationale.text: A Do Not Enter sign forbids entering that road or freeway, and seeing it usually means you are going the wrong way.

lines.text: Obey every official sign and signal.
Shape and color name the sign family.

narration.text: This lesson is about reading road signs quickly and knowing what each one asks of you. Start with the ground rule: you must obey every official sign, signal and pavement marking. The only exception is when a police officer or a road worker is directing traffic in a different way, and then you follow that person. Signs often use pictures or symbols instead of words, so you cannot always rely on reading them. Instead, each family of signs has its own color and its own shape. Once you know the families, you can tell what kind of rule is coming before you are close enough to read a single word.

lines.text: Red regulatory signs forbid actions.
They help control traffic through intersections.
Shape tells you which red rule applies.

narration.text: Red is the color of prohibitive regulatory signs. Their job is to forbid certain actions and to help control traffic moving through intersections. Within the red family, the shape does a lot of the work. The octagon, the eight-sided sign, means stop. The triangle means yield. The square red sign means Do Not Enter. Because each shape is tied to one rule, you can tell which rule applies from the outline alone, even from far away or when the words are hard to see. On a practice question, if a sign is described only by its shape and color, use the shape to name it first, then recall what the sign requires.

title.text: The stop sign, step by step

lines.text: Stop completely.
Yield to other vehicles.
Wait for anyone in a crosswalk.
Enter when it is safe.

narration.text: At an eight-sided stop sign, the rule has several parts, and all of them matter. First, come to a complete stop, not a rolling slowdown. Next, yield to other vehicles. Then wait for anyone in the crosswalk, and remember that this covers both a marked crosswalk with painted lines and an unmarked one at the corner. Only after all of that do you enter the intersection, and only when it is safe. A common twist in practice questions is a crosswalk with no paint. A walker in an unmarked crosswalk gets the same wait as one in a marked crosswalk, so the answer is still to stop and wait.

lines.text: Slow down and give the right of way.
Stop when needed, as at a stop sign.

narration.text: The triangular yield sign asks for something different from the stop sign. It means slow down and give the right of way to others. If giving the right of way requires it, you stop just as you would at a stop sign. So the key difference is when the stop happens. A stop sign always requires a full stop, every single time. A yield sign requires slowing and giving way, and a stop only when traffic or pedestrians make it necessary. If a question describes an empty cross street at a triangle, slowing and giving way is enough. At an octagon with the same empty street, you still stop completely.

lines.text: Square red Do Not Enter: you may be going the wrong way.
Red circle with a slash: the turn shown is not allowed.

narration.text: Two more red signs catch drivers out. The square Do Not Enter sign tells you not to enter that road or freeway. If you see one facing you, it usually means you are heading the wrong way, so do not continue. The other is a red circle with a slash across a turn symbol. You see it on No Left Turn, No Right Turn and No U Turn signs, and it means you may not make the turn the symbol shows. The trap is mixing the two. Do Not Enter bars the whole road ahead of you, while the circle with a slash bars only the one turn drawn inside the circle.

lines.text: A square red sign reads Do Not Enter on a ramp.
What is likely wrong?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are turning onto a ramp and a square red sign facing you reads Do Not Enter. What is most likely happening, and what should you do? Think about the shape first. The octagon is stop, the triangle is yield, and the square red sign is Do Not Enter. The answer is that you are probably heading the wrong way, and you must not enter that road or freeway. The sign does not ask you to stop and then go, and it does not ask you to slow down and give way. It tells you not to enter at all, and seeing it is a strong hint that your direction is wrong.

lines.text: An officer or road worker can override signs.
Octagon stop, triangle yield, square Do Not Enter.

narration.text: To wrap up, keep the ground rule in mind: obey every official sign, signal and marking unless a police officer or road worker directs traffic differently. Red signs forbid actions and help control traffic through intersections. Read the shape before the words. The octagon means a complete stop every time, with yielding and a wait for anyone in a crosswalk. The triangle means slow down and give way, stopping only if traffic or pedestrians make it necessary. The square red sign means Do Not Enter, and a red circle with a slash means the turn shown is off limits. Those ideas cover most red sign questions.

why_how.text: White rectangular signs tell you what to do and stand at or near the place where the rule applies.
Special lanes belong to particular users, so knowing who may use each one keeps you out of the wrong lane.

scenario.text: Leo is driving a car in a lane signed Right Lane Transit Only, and he needs a driveway on the next block where a Right Turns Permitted sign is posted.

reasoning.text: Ordinary cars may not go straight from the transit lane, but the Right Turns Permitted sign lets them use it briefly to reach a driveway.

result.text: Leo uses the lane only for the short stretch, yields to a bus in it, merges in behind the bus and turns into the driveway.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the middle lane marked Center Lane Turn Only is a carpool lane.

correction.text: The center lane is shared by left-turning drivers from both directions, while an HOV lane is reserved by how many people are in the vehicle.

prompt.text: A driver coming the other way is waiting in the middle lane marked Center Lane Turn Only. What is that driver doing?

answer.text: Waiting to turn left, because the lane is shared by left turners from both directions.

rationale.text: The Center Lane Turn Only lane is shared by left-turning drivers from both directions; it is not reserved by the number of riders like an HOV lane.

lines.text: White rectangles tell you what to do.
Some lanes belong to specific users.

narration.text: This lesson covers the white rectangular regulatory signs and the special lanes they control. Apart from the red signs, regulatory signs are rectangles with black words or symbols on a white background. They tell you what to do, and they stand at or near the place where the rule applies, so the rule usually starts right where you see the sign. Some of these signs also control lanes. Lane-use control signs show which lanes must turn and which lanes may turn at an intersection. Others reserve a lane for transit, for carpools, or for left turns. By the end, you will know who belongs in each lane.

lines.text: Speed limit is the maximum in miles per hour.
Electronic limits may change with conditions.
One way: travel only where the arrow points.

narration.text: Two of the most common white signs are the speed limit sign and the one way sign. A speed limit sign gives the maximum speed in miles per hour. It is a ceiling, not a target and not a suggestion. Some speed limit signs are electronic, and those may change with current conditions, so the number you saw yesterday may not be the number today. The one way sign is simpler still. On a one way road, traffic may travel only in the direction the arrow points. If a question asks whether you may drive against the arrow at any time, the answer is no, because the arrow alone sets the direction.

lines.text: Right Turn Permitted Without Stopping: right turners go.
Everyone else still stops and yields.
Do Not Pass forbids passing.
No Turn on Red: wait for green.

narration.text: Several white signs change how you turn or pass. A Right Turn Permitted Without Stopping sign is sometimes mounted under a stop sign. It lets traffic turning right go without stopping, but all other traffic must still stop and yield, so a driver going straight or turning left still stops. A Do Not Pass sign means passing is not allowed. A No Turn on Red sign means you must wait for the green signal before turning. Keep those last two apart: Do Not Pass forbids passing, while No Turn on Red forbids turning until the light turns green. Neither one is about the other's action.

title.text: Yield on green, stop for walkers

lines.text: Left Turn Yield on Green: yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
Stop Here for Pedestrians: stop at the stop line.
Keep Right: stay right of the island.

narration.text: A Left Turn Yield on Green sign is a reminder about the round green light. On a green circular light you may turn left, but you must yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians until the turn is safe. A Stop Here for Pedestrians sign stands near a crosswalk and means you stop at the stop line whenever someone is in that crosswalk, not inside the crosswalk itself. One more sign belongs here: a Keep Right sign warns that an island, a median or another obstruction splits the road ahead, and you stay to its right. Each of these tells you exactly where to be, or whom to wait for.

lines.text: Lane-use signs: which lanes must or may turn.
Center Lane Turn Only: left turns from both directions.
HOV lane: enough people on board, maybe a white diamond.

narration.text: Some lanes have owners. Lane-use control signs show which lanes must turn and which may turn at an intersection, so read them before you commit to a lane. A Center Lane Turn Only sign means the middle lane is shared by drivers turning left from both directions, so expect someone facing you in it. A high occupancy vehicle lane is reserved for vehicles carrying at least the number of people on the sign, such as two or more, and it may show a painted white diamond. The center lane is defined by the left turn, while the HOV lane is defined by how many people are in the vehicle.

lines.text: Transit Only: only transit, and shown bicycles, go straight.
Right Turns Permitted: brief use to turn or park.
Yield to buses and bikes, merge in behind.

narration.text: Transit lanes are where many drivers slip up. At a Right Lane Transit Only sign, only transit vehicles may continue straight through the intersection from that lane, along with bicycles when the sign shows them. An ordinary car may not go straight from that lane. A Right Turns Permitted sign changes things only a little. It lets you use the transit lane briefly to reach a driveway, the next intersection or legal curb parking. While you are in it, yield to buses and bikes and merge in behind them. The trap is treating brief use as permission to drive straight through, which the transit only rule forbids.

lines.text: A driver faces you in the Center Lane Turn Only lane.
What is that driver doing?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a busy road a driver coming the other way is waiting in the middle lane marked Center Lane Turn Only. What is that driver doing, and is it allowed? The answer is that the driver is waiting to turn left, and it is allowed. A Center Lane Turn Only lane is shared by left-turning drivers coming from both directions, so meeting someone facing you there is normal. It is not a carpool lane. A high occupancy vehicle lane is the one reserved by the number of people in the vehicle, sometimes with a painted white diamond, and it has nothing to do with left turns.

lines.text: The rule applies where the sign stands.
Know each lane's owner before you enter.

narration.text: Let us pull the white signs together. Regulatory rectangles carry black words or symbols on white and tell you what to do where they stand. The speed limit is the maximum, and electronic limits can change. One way roads run only in the direction of the arrow. Under a stop sign, a Right Turn Permitted Without Stopping sign frees only right turners. Do Not Pass forbids passing, and No Turn on Red makes you wait for green. Transit lanes carry only transit, and shown bikes, straight through, and HOV lanes need enough people aboard. Read the sign, then pick the lane it allows you.

why_how.text: Yellow warning signs give you time to adjust to a hazard or changed conditions before you reach it.
Signs for merging, added lanes and ending lanes call for different actions, so confusing them leads to the wrong move.

scenario.text: Sam drives in the right lane and passes a yellow Lane Reduction sign that marks his lane.

reasoning.text: A Lane Reduction sign means the marked lane ends and its drivers must merge, unlike an Add Lane sign, where two roads join and no merge is needed.

result.text: Sam merges into the through lane before his lane ends.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a Chevron sign warns of a curve somewhere further ahead.

correction.text: Curve and Sharp Turn signs warn of what lies ahead, but a Chevron sign marks the sharp curve or change of direction right at the sign.

memory_support.text: Ahead signs warn, chevrons mark the spot.

prompt.text: On a mountain road you reach yellow chevrons placed along the bend. Is the sharp curve still ahead, or right there?

rationale.text: A Chevron sign marks a sharp curve or change of direction at the sign itself, while Curve and Sharp Turn signs warn of what is ahead.

lines.text: Warning signs flag hazards or changes ahead.
React to conditions, signed or not.

narration.text: Yellow warning signs are your early notice. They flag possible hazards or changed conditions on the road ahead, giving you time to get ready before you reach them. But a warning sign is a courtesy, not a guarantee. You must react to the conditions in front of you whether or not a sign warned you about them. A missing sign never excuses driving into a hazard you can see. In this lesson you will work through the yellow signs about curves, about intersections, and about lanes that join, end or change direction, and for each one you will learn what it says lies ahead of you.

title.text: Curves ahead and at the spot

lines.text: Curve sign: a curve ahead.
Sharp Turn sign: a sharp turn ahead.
Chevron: the sharp curve is at the sign.

narration.text: Three signs deal with single bends. A Curve sign warns of a curve ahead, and a Sharp Turn sign warns of a sharp turn ahead. Both are advance warnings, so the bend is still to come when you pass them. A Chevron sign works differently. It marks a sharp curve or a change of direction right at the sign itself, so by the time you see chevrons, you are at the bend. That is the main contrast to remember: Curve and Sharp Turn signs tell you what lies ahead, while the Chevron marks the spot. Questions often swap these, so tie the Chevron to the bend itself.

lines.text: Winding Road: a series of turns or curves.
Reversing Curves: right, then left.

narration.text: Two more curve signs describe more than one bend. A Winding Road sign warns of a series of turns or curves, so expect the road to keep bending for a while. A Reversing Curves sign is more specific. It warns that the road bends right and then left, a single pair of curves in opposite directions. The easy way to hold them apart is to count. Winding Road means many curves, while Reversing Curves means one curve right followed by one curve left. When a question describes a road that bends one way and then right away the other, the sign is Reversing Curves, not Winding Road.

lines.text: Crossroad: four way intersection, cross traffic may enter.
Side Road: a T, traffic joins from left or right.
Divided Highway Begins or Ends: keep right.

narration.text: Some warnings are about intersections and road layout. A Crossroad sign warns of a four way intersection ahead, where cross traffic may enter your path. A Side Road sign warns of a T intersection, where traffic joins from the left or the right. The difference is whether the other road crosses yours completely or meets it from one side. A related pair of signs reads Divided Highway Begins and Divided Highway Ends. They mark where a divided highway starts or stops, and on a divided highway you keep to the right. Each of these tells you how the road ahead is shaped, so you can expect the traffic it brings.

lines.text: Merge: traffic joins from the side shown.
Add Lane: two roadways join, no merge needed.

narration.text: Where roads come together, read the sign carefully. A Merge sign warns that traffic is joining from the side shown, so expect vehicles to move into your road. An Add Lane sign looks like it is about joining too, but its meaning is different. It means two roadways join and a new lane is added, so no merge is needed and nobody has to squeeze in. In short, a Merge sign means traffic will join your road from the side shown, while an Add Lane sign means the roads join with a new lane. Practice questions often hinge on whether anyone must merge at all, so check which of the two you are facing.

lines.text: Lane Reduction: marked lane ends, merge into through lane.
Two-Way Traffic Ahead: oncoming traffic begins.

narration.text: Here is a pair that trips people up. A Lane Reduction sign means the marked lane ends soon, and drivers in that lane must merge into the through lane. If you are in the ending lane, the job of merging is yours. A Two-Way Traffic Ahead sign means something else entirely. Your one way road becomes a two way road, and you will meet oncoming traffic. One sign is about losing a lane beside you, and the other is about traffic coming toward you. The trap is treating them as the same warning. When the question says oncoming traffic, think Two-Way Traffic Ahead, and when it says merge, think Lane Reduction.

lines.text: Chevrons stand right at a bend.
Is the curve ahead, or here?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a mountain road you reach a row of yellow chevrons placed along the bend itself. Is the sharp curve still somewhere ahead of you, or is it right where the chevrons stand? The answer is that it is right there. A Chevron sign marks a sharp curve or a change of direction at the sign itself. The signs that warn of a bend still to come are the Curve sign and the Sharp Turn sign. So if the question places you at the chevrons, you are already at the curve, and if it places you at a Curve or Sharp Turn sign, the bend lies ahead.

title.text: Read the road before it arrives

lines.text: Curves: ahead signs versus chevrons at the spot.
Lanes: merge, added lane, lane ends, two way.

narration.text: To close, remember that yellow signs flag hazards and changes ahead, and that you must react to conditions whether or not a sign warns you. For curves, Curve and Sharp Turn warn ahead, chevrons mark the bend at the sign, Winding Road means a series of curves and Reversing Curves means right then left. For intersections, Crossroad is four way and Side Road is a T. For lanes, Merge means traffic joins from the side shown, Add Lane means no merge is needed, Lane Reduction means the marked lane ends, and Two-Way Traffic Ahead means oncoming traffic begins. Keep right on a divided highway.

why_how.text: Advance warning signs tell you to slow down and get ready before you reach a stop, a light or a lower limit.
Mixing up a coming legal limit with an advisory speed can lead you to treat the law as only a suggestion.

scenario.text: Ana passes a Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign on a highway, then later an Advisory Speed sign on an exit ramp.

reasoning.text: The first warns that a lower legal limit is coming, while the second only recommends a safe speed for the ramp.

result.text: Ana prepares to slow to the new legal limit, and on the ramp she keeps to the advised safe speed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a flashing beacon on a pedestrian crossing sign can be ignored when nobody is in the crosswalk yet.

correction.text: The flashing yellow beacon means someone is crossing now, has just crossed or is about to cross.

memory_support.text: Ahead signs buy time to slow.

prompt.text: On a curving exit ramp a sign shows a recommended speed. Is it a coming legal limit or safe speed advice?

answer.text: It is advice: an Advisory Speed sign gives the safe speed for the ramp or curve.

rationale.text: A lower legal limit is announced by a Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign, while an Advisory Speed sign only recommends a safe speed.

lines.text: Advance warnings name what is coming.
Slow down and prepare before you arrive.

narration.text: Many yellow signs exist to buy you time. They name something that is coming so you can slow down and prepare before you get there. A Stop Ahead sign warns of a stop sign ahead, so you slow down and get ready to stop. A Signal Ahead sign means slow down and be prepared to stop for a traffic light. A Roundabout Ahead sign announces a roundabout intersection, and a Railroad Advance sign warns of a railroad crossing where you may need to stop. In each case the sign is not the place to act. It is the reminder that the place to act is just ahead of you.

lines.text: Flashing beacon: someone is crossing, just crossed or is about to.
Multiuse Path Crossing: cyclists and walkers cross here.
In-Street Pedestrian Crossing: stop for anyone in the crosswalk.

narration.text: Pedestrian warnings need extra attention. A pedestrian crossing sign may carry a flashing yellow beacon. When it flashes, someone is crossing now, has just crossed or is about to cross, so expect a person in or near the crosswalk even if you cannot see one yet. A Multiuse Path Crossing sign marks a place where cyclists and walkers often cross the road. An In-Street Pedestrian Crossing sign means you stop when someone is in the crosswalk. These signs share one message: people on foot or on bikes are likely to be in your path, and you need to be ready for them.

lines.text: Reduced Speed Limit Ahead: a lower legal limit is coming.
Advisory Speed: a safe speed for a ramp or curve.
Advisory signs may be electronic and change.

narration.text: Two speed signs look related but carry different weight. A Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign means prepare to slow to a lower limit, and that lower limit is a legal one. An Advisory Speed sign gives the safe speed for a freeway ramp or a curve. It may be paired with other signs, and it may be electronic and change with conditions. The contrast to keep is simple. The reduced limit sign warns that a lower legal limit is coming, while the advisory sign only recommends a safe speed for the ramp or curve. One is a coming law, and the other is advice about a safe speed.

lines.text: Stop Ahead: a stop sign is coming.
Signal Ahead: a traffic light is coming.

narration.text: A frequent trap is swapping the Stop Ahead sign with the Signal Ahead sign. Both ask you to slow down and get ready to stop, so the action feels the same. The difference is what waits for you. A Stop Ahead sign warns of a stop sign ahead, which means a stop is coming no matter what. A Signal Ahead sign warns of a traffic light ahead, where you must be prepared to stop if the light requires it. When a question asks what you will find at the intersection, choose the stop sign for Stop Ahead and the traffic light for Signal Ahead. Do not stop at the warning sign itself.

lines.text: Low Clearance: too tall means do not continue.
Hill: a steep grade ahead.
Slippery When Wet: slick in rain.
Deer: slow if you see wildlife.

narration.text: Some warnings are about the road itself or what lives near it. A Low Clearance sign means the overpass ahead is low. If your vehicle is too tall to fit beneath it, do not continue. A Hill sign warns of a steep grade ahead. A Slippery When Wet sign means the pavement becomes unusually slick in rain, so a stretch that feels easy when dry can be much harder in a storm. A Deer sign means deer often cross there, so slow down if you see deer or other wildlife. Each sign names a specific condition, and the right response follows from that condition, not from the color alone.

lines.text: A ramp sign shows a recommended speed.
Law coming, or advice?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a curving freeway exit ramp, a sign shows a recommended speed for the ramp. Is that number a lower legal limit coming up, or advice about a safe speed? The answer is that it is advice. An Advisory Speed sign gives the safe speed for a freeway ramp or curve, and it may be electronic and change with conditions. The sign that warns of a lower legal limit is a different one, the Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign, which tells you to prepare to slow to that limit. So a ramp or curve with a recommended speed points to advisory, while a coming limit points to the law.

lines.text: Prepare for stops, lights, roundabouts and rails.
Watch for walkers, cyclists and wildlife.

narration.text: To finish, think of these signs as a preview of the next stretch of road. Stop Ahead and Signal Ahead mean slow down and get ready to stop. Reduced Speed Limit Ahead means a lower legal limit is coming, while an Advisory Speed sign recommends a safe speed for a ramp or curve. Roundabout Ahead and Railroad Advance announce what kind of crossing is next. A flashing beacon on a pedestrian sign means someone is crossing, has crossed or is about to. Low Clearance, Hill, Slippery When Wet and Deer signs each name a condition you must be ready for before you reach it.

why_how.text: Route and guide signs tell you which road you are on and help you pick the right exit.
Sign color tells you the kind of destination, so green, brown and blue lead to different places.

scenario.text: Kim needs fuel and then wants to visit a state park.

reasoning.text: Fuel is a motorist service shown on blue signs, while parks are shown on brown signs.

result.text: Kim follows the blue sign to the gas station and then the brown sign to the park.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a sign pointing to a hospital is a green guide sign.

correction.text: A blue sign to a hospital is a motorist service sign, in the same family as fuel, food, lodging, rest areas, charging and accessible parking.

memory_support.text: Green goes, brown explores, blue serves.

prompt.text: You want to stop at a picnic ground off the highway. Which sign color should you follow?

rationale.text: Brown signs point to historic and cultural places as well as scenic areas, picnic grounds and parks, while green signs lead to exits, roads and cities.

lines.text: Route signs name your road.
Color tells the kind of destination.

narration.text: Not every sign is a rule or a warning. Some simply help you find your way. Route signs tell you which road you are on and whether it is an interstate, a U.S. route or a state highway. Beyond that, color does most of the work. Green signs guide you to exits, roads and cities. Brown signs point to historic, cultural and recreation sites. Blue signs show services for motorists. In this short lesson you will learn what each color leads to, how exit numbers help you, and what a safety corridor sign asks you to do. Knowing the colors lets you plan a move well before the exit arrives.

lines.text: Green guide signs give exit details.
They point to roads and cities.
The exit number helps you choose.

narration.text: Green guide signs, also called information signs, give exit details and point the way to roads and cities. On a freeway they are how you find the turnoff you need. Each exit has a number, and that number helps you choose the right exit, especially when several exits come close together. Pair that with the route signs, which tell you which road you are on and whether it is an interstate, a U.S. route or a state highway. Together they answer two questions: where am I, and where do I get off. If a question asks which sign helps you pick an exit, think green and the exit number.

lines.text: Brown: historic, cultural, scenic, picnic and park sites.
Blue: gas, food, lodging, rest areas, charging, hospital.

narration.text: Brown and blue signs point to places you might want, rather than to cities. Brown signs point to historic and cultural places as well as scenic areas, picnic grounds and parks. Blue signs are motorist service signs. They show gas, food, lodging, rest areas, electric vehicle charging, and accessible facilities or parking, and they show the way to a hospital. That last item matters, because a hospital sign is easy to file under guide signs. It belongs in the blue motorist service family, alongside fuel, food, lodging, rest areas, charging and accessible parking. Brown means things to see, while blue means things you need.

lines.text: A hospital sign is blue, not green.
Parks are brown, cities are green.

narration.text: The trap in this topic is mixing the colors. Many drivers assume any sign giving directions must be green. Green signs do guide you to exits, roads and cities, but they are not the only signs that point somewhere. Brown signs point to historic, cultural and recreation sites, so a park, a picnic ground or a scenic area will be on brown. A blue sign pointing to a hospital is a motorist service sign, not a guide sign, and it sits in the same family as fuel, food and lodging. When a question names a destination, match it to the color first, and the answer usually follows.

lines.text: You want a picnic ground off the highway.
Which sign color do you follow?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are on a long highway drive and want to stop at a picnic ground. Which sign color should you watch for? The answer is brown. Brown signs point to historic and cultural places as well as scenic areas, picnic grounds and parks. Green signs would lead you to exits, roads and cities, which is not what you need here. Blue signs show services such as gas, food, lodging, rest areas and charging. So for a picnic ground or a park, follow brown, and for the next city or the right exit number, follow green guide signs instead.

lines.text: Safety corridor: turn your lights on.
Green guides, brown explores, blue serves.

narration.text: One more sign belongs with the guide signs. Safety corridors are designated stretches of highway with more fatal and serious injury crashes than the statewide average. When you are in one, turn your lights on. Their signs may carry diamond-shaped flags, which help them stand out. To wrap up the colors: route signs tell you the road and its type, green guide signs give exits and directions to roads and cities, brown signs point to historic, cultural and recreation sites, and blue signs show motorist services, including the way to a hospital. Match the color to the destination and you will rarely pick the wrong sign.

title.text: Red lights and turns on red

why_how.text: A steady red and a flashing red ask for different things, so knowing which you face tells you whether to wait or go after stopping.
Turning on red is allowed only in certain directions after a full stop, so knowing the limits keeps you from an illegal turn.

scenario.text: Raj stops at a red light and wants to turn left onto a one way street whose traffic flows to the left.

reasoning.text: After a complete stop on red, a left turn is allowed only onto a one way road in its direction of travel, unless a sign or officer forbids it.

result.text: With no sign or officer forbidding it, Raj may make the left turn after his complete stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a dark signal during a power outage lets the busier road keep going.

correction.text: A dark signal means stop as if every approach had a stop sign, the same way you treat a flashing red.

memory_support.text: Steady red stays, flashing red is a stop sign.

prompt.text: After a full stop at a red light, may you turn left onto a two way street?

answer.text: No. A left on red is allowed only onto a one way road going in the direction of the turn.

rationale.text: Right on red onto a two way road is allowed after a full stop, but left on red needs a one way road traveling the way you turn.

lines.text: Steady red: stop and stay stopped.
Flashing red: treat it like a stop sign.

narration.text: This lesson is about red lights, and the first job is to notice whether the red is steady or flashing. A steady circular red light means stop and stay stopped until the signal changes. A flashing red light is different: it is treated exactly like a stop sign, so you stop and then proceed as you would at a stop sign. Later in the lesson you will see what to do when a signal is dark or broken, which turns are allowed after stopping on red, and how a red arrow fits in. Many red light questions turn on one word, steady or flashing, so look for it first.

lines.text: Stop at a steady circular red.
Stay stopped until the signal changes.

narration.text: A steady circular red light means stop, and it also means stay stopped until the signal changes. That second part is what separates it from a stop sign. At a stop sign you stop, yield and then go when safe, but at a steady red you wait for the light itself to change before going straight ahead. A flashing red light, on the other hand, is treated like a stop sign. So the contrast is simple. Steady red means stop and stay stopped until it changes, while flashing red means stop and then proceed as at a stop sign. Hold onto that, because the turn rules build on the steady red.

lines.text: Dark signal: stop as if every approach had a stop sign.
Flashing signal: obey its flashing meaning.

narration.text: Sometimes a signal is not working. If a signal is dark, as in a power outage, stop as if every approach had a stop sign. That means every driver at the intersection stops, no matter which road is busier. A flashing red light or a dark signal is treated exactly like a stop sign. A broken signal that is flashing, rather than dark, is obeyed by its flashing meaning. If it flashes red, treat it as a stop sign. If it flashes yellow, follow what a flashing yellow light means. The short version is easy to keep: dark means stop at every approach, and flashing means obey the color that flashes.

lines.text: Complete stop first.
Right onto a two way road.
Right or left onto a one way road, with its flow.
Not if a sign or officer forbids it.

narration.text: You may turn on a red light, but only after a complete stop and only in certain directions. Unless a sign or an officer forbids it, you may turn right onto a two way road. You may also turn right or left onto a one way road, as long as you turn in its direction of travel. Notice what is missing from that list: a left turn on red onto a two way road. That is not allowed. So right on red works onto a two way road after a full stop, but a left on red works only onto a one way road going the direction of your turn. A sign or an officer can take away even these turns.

lines.text: Left on red needs a one way road.
It must flow the way you turn.

narration.text: Here is where many drivers go wrong. They learn that right on red is allowed and assume left on red works the same way. It does not. Turning right on red onto a two way road is allowed after a full stop. A left turn on red is allowed only onto a one way road going in the direction of the turn. If the street on your left carries traffic both ways, you wait for the signal to change. If it is a one way street flowing to your left, a left on red is allowed after a complete stop, unless a sign or an officer forbids it. Check the street, not just the light.

lines.text: You stopped fully at a red light.
May you turn left onto a two way street?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you have come to a complete stop at a red light and want to turn left onto a two way street. No sign or officer says anything about turning. May you go? The answer is no. A left turn on red is allowed only onto a one way road going in the direction of the turn, and a two way street does not qualify. A right turn onto that same two way street would be allowed after the full stop. The same limits hold if the signal shows a steady red arrow instead of a red ball, because the turns allowed on a steady red are also allowed on a red arrow.

lines.text: Steady red or red arrow: stop and stay.
Flashing red or dark: treat as a stop sign.

narration.text: To close, sort red lights by what they ask. A steady circular red light means stop and stay stopped until it changes. A steady red arrow means the same, stop and stay stopped until it changes, but the same turns allowed on a steady red light are allowed on the red arrow. A flashing red light or a dark signal is treated exactly like a stop sign, and a dark signal means every approach stops. After a complete stop on red, unless a sign or officer forbids it, you may turn right onto a two way road, or right or left onto a one way road in its direction of travel.

why_how.text: Yellow lights tell you whether red is coming or caution is needed, so reading them right decides whether you stop.
Whether a green gives you the right of way depends on whether it is an arrow or a circle.

scenario.text: Jo waits to turn left on a flashing yellow arrow while oncoming traffic has a steady green.

reasoning.text: A flashing yellow arrow allows the turn only after yielding to pedestrians and oncoming traffic, unlike a steady yellow arrow, which warns the movement is ending.

result.text: Jo lets the oncoming cars and a pedestrian go first, then makes the turn.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a steady yellow light means speed up to get through before red.

correction.text: A steady yellow tells you to stop before the intersection if you safely can, and to continue carefully only if you cannot stop safely.

memory_support.text: Arrow protects, ball makes you yield.

prompt.text: A left arrow changes from green to steady yellow just before you enter. What is it telling you?

answer.text: The arrow is about to turn red, so stop before entering, or go carefully if stopping is unsafe.

rationale.text: A steady yellow arrow warns that the protected movement is ending, unlike a flashing yellow arrow, which allows a turn after yielding.

lines.text: Steady or flashing changes the meaning.
Arrow or circle changes the right of way.

narration.text: Yellow and green lights look simple, but two details change their meaning. The first is whether the light is steady or flashing. A steady circular yellow warns that red is coming, while a flashing yellow means slow down and go ahead with caution. The second detail is whether you are looking at a circle or an arrow. A green arrow gives you the right of way for the movement it shows, while a circular green permits the movement but makes a left turn yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic. In this lesson you will work through each of these lights and arrows and what each one lets you do.

lines.text: Steady yellow: red is coming, stop if you safely can.
Cannot stop safely: continue carefully.
Flashing yellow: slow down, go with caution.

narration.text: A steady circular yellow light warns that red is coming. Your job is to stop before the intersection. If you cannot stop safely, continue carefully through it. Compare that with a steady red light, which requires you to stop and stay stopped with no such option. The steady yellow gives you that choice only when stopping is unsafe. A flashing yellow light is different again. It does not warn of a coming red. It means slow down and go ahead with caution. So steady yellow is about stopping if you safely can, while flashing yellow is about slowing down and proceeding with care.

lines.text: Steady yellow arrow: about to turn red.
Flashing yellow arrow: turn after yielding.
Oncoming traffic has a steady green.

narration.text: Arrows add a layer. A steady yellow arrow warns that the arrow is about to turn red. Stop before entering, or if stopping is unsafe, go carefully through, much as with a steady yellow ball. A flashing yellow arrow means something else. It allows the turn the arrow shows, but only after you yield to pedestrians and to oncoming traffic, and that oncoming traffic has a steady green light. So a steady yellow arrow tells you the protected movement is ending, while a flashing yellow arrow permits the turn once you have yielded. The word flashing is the clue that you may turn.

lines.text: Steady green: straight, left or right unless a sign forbids.
Left turns yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic.
Right turns yield to pedestrians.
Green arrow: your right of way.

narration.text: A steady green light allows you to go straight, turn left or turn right, unless a sign forbids one of those moves. But a green ball does not hand you the right of way over everyone. A left turn must yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic, and a right turn must yield to pedestrians. A steady green arrow is stronger. It gives you the right of way to make the movement the arrow shows. That is the contrast to remember: a green arrow gives you the right of way for the movement shown, while a circular green permits the movement but a left turn must still yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic.

lines.text: Steady yellow: stop if you safely can.
Continue only when stopping is unsafe.

narration.text: A common mistake is treating a steady yellow light as a signal to speed up and get through before red. The rule points the other way. A steady circular yellow light warns that red is coming, so you stop before the intersection. Only if you cannot stop safely do you continue, and then you go carefully through it. A steady red is stricter still: stop and stay stopped until it changes. So the yellow gives you a narrow exception for when stopping is unsafe, not a reason to hurry. When a practice question offers speeding up as an option at a yellow light, it is the wrong choice.

lines.text: Your green arrow turns steady yellow.
What is it warning you about?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are about to turn left on a green arrow when it changes to a steady yellow arrow before you enter. What is it telling you, and what should you do? The answer is that the arrow is about to turn red. Stop before entering, or if stopping is unsafe, go carefully through. A steady yellow arrow warns that the protected movement is ending. It is not the same as a flashing yellow arrow, which allows the turn only after you yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic. Steady means the protection is ending, while flashing means you may turn after yielding.

title.text: Who has the right of way

lines.text: Green arrow protects your turn.
Green ball and flashing yellow arrow make you yield.

narration.text: To finish, line the lights up by who has the right of way. A steady green arrow gives you the right of way for the movement it shows. A steady green ball lets you go straight, left or right unless a sign forbids it, but left turns yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic, and right turns yield to pedestrians. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn only after yielding to pedestrians and oncoming traffic, which has a steady green. A flashing yellow ball means slow down and go ahead with caution. A steady yellow, ball or arrow, means red is next, so stop if you safely can.
